source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / ASPIRE Project, IFAD-funded - "ដំណាំក្រូចថ្លុង" (Pomelo Cultivation Guide), 2017, 90pp
text:
The source dedicates specific attention to natural enemies that help keep citrus pests, especially psyllid and aphid/scale populations, in check without pesticide use. Named beneficial species include the parasitic wasps Diaphorencyrtus aligarhensis and Tamarixia radiata (both attacking Asian citrus psyllid nymphs - the source notes Tamarixia radiata alone can parasitize a large share, on the order of 70%, of psyllid nymphs in some observations, versus roughly 30% for Diaphorencyrtus aligarhensis), a six-spotted ladybird beetle (Menochilus sexmaculatus, family Coccinellidae) which preys on aphids and other soft-bodied pests, weaver ants (អង្រែង, Oecophylla smaragdina) which, despite also protecting some sap-sucking pests for their honeydew, prey on caterpillars and other pests, and various spiders (families Oxyopidae, Linyphiidae, Salticidae, Theridiosomatidae, Thomisidae and others) that prey generally on small insect pests in the canopy.

Because these natural enemies provide free, ongoing pest suppression, the source recommends managing the orchard in ways that protect them - for example limiting broad-spectrum insecticide use, which can kill beneficial insects along with the target pest and allow pest populations to rebound faster than their natural enemies can recover.
